lessons.title: a_e (VCe with a)
lessons.goal: Read and spell words with the vowel-consonant-e pattern using **a**, where a silent final e makes the vowel "say its name" (/ā/).
lessons.review: all Level 1–2 letters, digraphs, blends, closed syllables, suffixes -s/-es/-ed/-ing/-er
lessons.heartLine: once, only (first two of the 16 Level 3 heart words — canonical schedule teaches 2/lesson through L3.08)

A.text: Jane and Kate are at the lake. / Jane has a cane. / Kate has a cape. / They skate on the lake. / Once, Kate got a cramp. / Jane came and gave Kate a hand. / Kate said, "Thank you, Jane!" / They made a plan to skate again.

B.text: Jake has a case to take to the bank. / He made a plane trip. / At the gate, he got a snack and a cake. / Jake's plane was late, but he was not sad. / He said, "I have cash." / Jake sat and had a nap. / Once the plane came, he got on fast.

listen.passage: A long time ago, people who wanted to send a message far away used pigeons. A trained pigeon could find its way home from a hundred miles off. Today we call sending a fast, important message 'urgent' — it means it cannot wait.

tier2.def: something urgent needs attention right away, it can't wait.
tier2.full: something urgent needs attention right away, it can't wait.

questions: How did people send fast messages before phones?
What makes something "urgent" instead of just "important"?

rule.title: Silent e
rule.text: The e at the end is silent. It jumps over one consonant and makes the vowel say its name: cap, cape.

lessons.title: i_e (VCe with i)
lessons.goal: Read and spell VCe words with **i** (long /ī/).

A.text: Mike has a bike. / He likes to ride it. / Mike and his dog Spike go for a ride. / Once, Mike's bike went flat. / Mike did not stop. / He got off and did a quick fix. / Spike sat still. / "Only a bit," said Mike, and they went back.

B.text: Kate got a bike to save time. / She rides it to her job many times. / At nine, she locks the bike and clocks in. / Once, the bike would not go, and Kate had to get off and push it. / She was not glad, but she did not quit. / Only a quick fix did it, and the next ride was fine.

listen.passage: Before bikes had rubber tires, riders used wheels with iron rims. Every bump in the road shook the whole bike — people called it a 'bone-shaker.' A ride that should have felt smooth instead felt rough and tiring.

tier2.def: not smooth; bumpy or hard to deal with.
tier2.full: not smooth; bumpy or hard to deal with.

questions: Why did old bikes feel rough to ride?
What's the difference between rough and smooth?

rule.title: Silent e
rule.text: i_e: the e is silent and the i says its name: kit, kite.

lessons.title: o_e, u_e, e_e (VCe with o, u, e)
lessons.goal: Complete the VCe set — read and spell words with o_e (/ō/), u_e (/o͞o/ or /ū/), and e_e (rare, /ē/).
lessons.newToday: o_e (home, rope), u_e — two sounds: /o͞o/ (rule, June) and /ū/ (cute, mule); e_e (these, Steve — rare, flag it)

A.text: Steve moved to a home. / It is big, and it has a gate. / Steve rode his bike home and did a jig. / He is very glad. / At home, Steve has a cute pet mule named Duke. / Duke likes a plate of grass. / "This home is very fine," said Steve, and he made a note to tell his pal.

B.text: Steve got home very late from his shift. / His job is to help sick kids, and the shift ran long. / At home, he made a snack and sat next to the stove. / His wife left a note: "I made a plate for you." / Steve smiled. / It was a very long shift, but home felt like a rest at last.

listen.passage: Mules are often used on farms because they are known to be very sturdy. A mule can carry a heavy load over rough ground for a long time without tiring, which makes it a reliable partner for farm work.

tier2.def: something or someone you can count on, again and again.
tier2.full: something or someone you can count on, again and again.

questions: Why are mules useful on farms?
What makes a person reliable?

rule.title: Silent e
rule.text: o_e, u_e and e_e work the same way: hop, hope; cub, cube.

lessons.title: VCe + the Drop-e Rule
lessons.goal: Apply the drop-e spelling rule when adding a vowel suffix (-ing, -ed, -er) to a VCe word: hope→hoping.
lessons.newToday: drop-e rule (spelling rule, no new grapheme)
lessons.review: a_e, i_e, o_e, u_e, e_e; -ing/-ed/-er suffixes (Level 2, no-base-change words)

A.text: Sam is making a kite. / He is using tape and a stick. / Every bit has to be just so. / Sam is smiling at his plan. / Once it is done, Sam is hoping for a fine time. / He is saving his kite for the big game. / "I made this alone," said Sam, very glad.

B.text: At the end of every shift, Kate is closing the shop at nine. / She is checking the till and saving the cash. / Once the till is closed, she is locking every gate. / Kate is not rushing — she likes taking her time. / "I am making it safe," she said, smiling at her plan for a safe close.

listen.passage: A shopkeeper's closing routine matters because a rushed close can leave a door unlocked or cash uncounted. A careful routine, done the same way every night, reduces the chance of a costly mistake.

tier2.def: a set of steps you do the same way, again and again.
tier2.full: a set of steps you do the same way, again and again.

questions: Why does a careful closing routine matter?
What's a routine you never skip?

check.note: learner writes the -ing form (dictation) and reads it (tap gate)

rule.title: Drop the e
rule.text: Before an ending that starts with a vowel (-ing, -ed, -er), drop the silent e: hope, hoping.

lessons.title: Open Syllables
lessons.goal: Read single-letter open syllables (he, go, hi, me — a single vowel at the end of a word/syllable says its long sound) and two-syllable open+closed words (ro-bot, mu-sic) using V/CV division.
lessons.newToday: open syllable long vowels (a e i o u alone at a syllable's end = long)

A.text: We go to spot a tiger. / The tiger is silent as it moves. / Because he had a project, a pupil at his class made a robot tiger. / It has one eye that shines. / "This is a great robot!" said the pupil. / We are so glad we came. / We go home and hum a tune, glad for the tigers.

B.text: Kate got a spot in a great program at her job site. / Because there were big tasks, she and the others made a robot to help. / The program runs a set of steps, silent and fast, no fuss. / "We tested it with one eye on the clock," said Kate. / The robot has done every task well. / Kate is glad she got to do this.

listen.passage: Engineers who design robots must consider every possible task the machine will face, because a robot cannot adapt on its own the way a person can. A well-designed robot follows a precise set of instructions, and even a small gap in those instructions can cause a big mistake.

tier2.def: exact, with no room for error.
tier2.full: exact, with no room for error.

questions: Why can't a robot adapt the way a person can?
When does being precise matter most in your life?

rule.title: Open syllables
rule.text: A syllable that ends with a vowel is open: the vowel says its name. Try the first vowel open: ro·bot, mu·sic.

lessons.title: Y as a Vowel
lessons.goal: Read words where final **y** acts as a vowel: /ē/ in multisyllable words (happy, funny) and /ī/ in one-syllable words (my, fly, cry).
lessons.newToday: y = /ē/ (end of longer words), y = /ī/ (end of one-syllable words)

A.text: My puppy is very busy. / He runs and hops in the sun by the shed. / My puppy is funny — when he digs in the mud, he gets sticky and muddy. / "Silly puppy!" I said, and gave him a rub. / We go home, and my puppy is happy because he is with me.

B.text: My shift was very busy, because I ran from the front to the back and did not stop by lunch. / When I got back, there was a note from a happy person: "Thank you, you made me very glad." / I am busy, but I am glad I had a busy, happy shift.

listen.passage: A customer who takes the time to leave a kind note is showing genuine gratitude — a real, felt thanks, not just a quick 'thanks' said out of habit. Genuine gratitude tends to stick with a person much longer than a routine thank-you.

tier2.def: a strong feeling of thanks for something someone did.
tier2.full: a strong feeling of thanks for something someone did.

questions: Why does a written note stick with someone longer than a quick "thanks"?
Who deserves your gratitude this week?

rule.title: Y as a vowel
rule.text: At the end of a short word y says /ī/: my. At the end of a longer word it says /ē/: happy.

lessons.title: Soft c, Soft g
lessons.goal: Read words where c says /s/ (soft c, before e/i/y) and g says /j/ (soft g, before e/i/y), plus the endings -ce, -ge, -dge.
lessons.newToday: soft c (city, ice), soft g (gem, cage), -ce, -ge, -dge

A.text: In the city, there is a big bridge. / Many people cross it often. / Once, my class went on a trip to visit it, because it is huge and made of stage-like steps. / When we got to the edge, we could spot a huge cage with a pet inside. / "So nice!" said the people, very glad. / We had a fine time at the bridge.

B.text: Since the bridge in the city closed, many people had to change the plan. / Many people came to fix it, page by page of a plan they had made. / "It is a huge job, but it is not a bad job if we take the time to do it well," said the judge. / People are glad the bridge will be fine once it is fixed.

listen.passage: Engineers who inspect a bridge look for tiny cracks long before the bridge is actually in danger of failing. Catching a problem early, while it is still minor, is far cheaper and safer than waiting until it becomes a crisis.
questions: Why is catching a problem early better than waiting?
What's the difference between a minor and a major problem?

rule.title: Soft c and soft g
rule.text: Before e, i or y, c says /s/ and g usually says /j/: city, cage. After a short vowel, /j/ is spelled -dge: bridge.

lessons.title: ar
lessons.goal: Read and spell words with r-controlled **ar** (/ar/, as in car, farm, start) — the first r-controlled vowel, taught here (matching UFLI/RWI sequencing) before any vowel team so common everyday words stop leaking into earlier lessons.
lessons.review: VCe (all 5 vowels), drop-e, open syllables, y=/ē//ī/, soft c/g, -ce/-ge/-dge
lessons.heartLine: whole, earth (last two of the 16 Level 3 heart words — all Level 3 heart words are now taught)

A.text: Sam and his mom go to the farm. / A big, red barn is at the farm. / Sam pets a cute pup and a fat pig. / "A big cart!" said Sam. / He rides in the cart with his mom, because he likes it a lot. / They spot a hen in the yard. / Once they are done, they have a snack of grapes. / Sam has a whole, fine time at the farm.

B.text: Kate got a job at the market. / She helps at a cart that sells fresh grapes and plums. / At nine, she sets up the cart and starts her shift. / "This job is hard, but I like it," said Kate. / She helps many people at the market, because she likes to help. / Once her shift is done, Kate has a snack and a cup of milk. / She has a whole, fine time at the market.

listen.passage: Farmers markets let shoppers buy food directly from the people who grew it, which often means the produce is fresher than what has traveled a long distance to a big store. Buying this way also supports the local economy.

tier2.def: the way money and goods move around in a place — who earns it, who spends it, who it helps.
tier2.full: the way money and goods move around in a place — who earns it, who spends it, who it helps.

questions: Why might food from a farmers market be fresher?
What's one small way people can support their local economy?

lessons.title: or, ore
lessons.goal: Read and spell words with r-controlled **or** (for, corn, short) and **ore** (more, store, before).
lessons.heartLine: none new — all 16 Level 3 heart words were completed at L3.08; today is decoding-only.

A.text: At the farm, Sam spots a horse. / The horse has a short, dark mane. / "Can I ride the horse?" asked Sam. / "Yes, hold on well," said his mom. / Sam gets on, and the horse trots because he holds on well. / Sam has a fun, short ride. / Once he is done, Sam pets the horse and says, "Thank you." / Sam has a whole, fine time at the farm.

B.text: Kate has a list, so she goes to the store. / She gets corn, milk, and a snack from a stand. / Before she is done, she checks her list. / "I got what I came for," said Kate. / She goes to the front and gets a short line. / She is glad she made a trip to the store, because she got what she came for.

listen.passage: Before horses could be domesticated for riding, humans had to build a relationship of trust with an animal that is naturally alert to danger. A horse that trusts its rider will respond calmly even in a busy, noisy place.

tier2.def: tamed and cared for by people, instead of living wild.
tier2.full: tamed and cared for by people, instead of living wild.

questions: Why do horses need to trust their rider?
What's the difference between a wild animal and a domesticated one?

lessons.title: ai, ay
lessons.goal: Read and spell the long-a vowel team spelled **ai** (mid-word) and **ay** (end of word).

A.text: It is play day at the park. / When rain starts, the class does not stay in — they play in the rain, and get wet from top to tail! / A snail comes on the wet path. / "There is a snail!" said Sam. / They wait for the rain to stop, then drink cold water and play again.

B.text: Every day, Kate takes the train to her job. / Today, because rain made the stop wet, the train came late. / She had to wait, so she got a cup of hot water and a snack from a stand. / "I will just wait," she said to a man in line. / The train came, and Kate got a spot by chance.

listen.passage: When trains are delayed during heavy rain, it is often because water can seep into the electrical system that controls the tracks, forcing a temporary shutdown until it is safe again.

tier2.def: lasting only for a short time, not permanent.
tier2.full: lasting only for a short time, not permanent.

questions: Why do trains sometimes stop running in heavy rain?
What's something in your life that was temporary but felt long?

lessons.title: ee, ea
lessons.goal: Read and spell the long-e vowel team spelled **ee** and **ea**.
lessons.review: ai, ay, open-syllable long e (he, we, me)

A.text: Sam and his team go to the beach. / When they see a green kite, they find a sweet, clean spot to sit. / "Let's eat lunch by the sea," said Sam. / They read a page and laugh at a funny bit. / A queen bee comes to see the sweet leaf, then goes home. / Sam and his team feel very happy after a fine day.

B.text: Each week, Kate and her team clean the street by the shop. / When they meet at nine, each one has a task. / Kate likes to see the street stay neat when they are done. / "We laugh a lot, but we get the job done," said Kate. / At the end, the team sits and has a sweet snack, glad for a job well done.

listen.passage: Communities that organize regular street clean-ups tend to build a stronger sense of civic pride, because neighbors who work side by side start to feel a shared responsibility for the place they live.

tier2.def: a duty or job that is yours to take care of.
tier2.full: a duty or job that is yours to take care of.

questions: Why might a clean-up build civic pride?
What responsibility do you take seriously?

lessons.title: oa, ow, oe
lessons.goal: Read and spell the long-o vowel team spelled **oa** (mid-word), **ow** (often end-word), and **oe** (rare, end-word).
lessons.review: ai/ay, ee/ea; open-syllable long o (go, so, no)

A.text: Sam and his dad walk to the pond with a fine boat. / When snow starts, the pond starts to glow white. / Because it is chilly, Sam puts on his coat and gets a snack of toast. / "Let's float the boat and see if it can go," said Dad. / The boat does float, and Sam claps and laughs. / They walk home, glad they came to play.

B.text: Kate had to walk home since the road was slow with traffic. / She put on her coat, since it was chilly, and got a snack of toast at a stand. / Another man said, "This road is always slow at this time." / Kate did not mind — she got to see the snow glow as she walked. / By the time she got home, she felt glad.

listen.passage: Traffic engineers study patterns in road congestion to figure out which streets need a second lane or a new signal. A small change, like a longer green light, can noticeably ease a slow commute for thousands of people.

tier2.def: in a way you can clearly see or notice.
tier2.full: in a way you can clearly see or notice.

questions: How can one small change ease traffic for many people?
What's something that changed noticeably for you recently?

lessons.title: igh, ie
lessons.goal: Read and spell the long-i vowel team spelled **igh** and **ie**.
lessons.review: i_e (same sound, different spelling), y=/ī/ (my, fly)

A.text: At night, Sam and his mom talk and gaze up at the sky. / Because the sky is bright, it glows white and high. / "Let's stay up a bit," said Mom. / They eat a slice of pie and talk of the sky. / Sam feels glad for this quiet, bright night with his mom.

B.text: After a long shift, Kate and her friend Jane talk it over at night. / When they sit and gaze up, the sky is bright. / "I might take the job at another site," said Kate. / Jane said, "That is a big thing — talk to your team, then decide." / They eat a slice of pie and talk until it gets late.

listen.passage: Talking through a big decision with someone you trust often reveals a perspective you had not considered on your own. A friend can point out a risk or an option you were too close to the problem to notice.

tier2.def: a way of looking at or thinking about something.
tier2.full: a way of looking at or thinking about something.

questions: Why can a friend see something you can't see about your own choice?
Who gives you a helpful perspective when you're deciding something?

lessons.title: ue, ew, ui
lessons.goal: Read and spell the vowel teams **ue**, **ew**, and **ui**, which usually say /o͞o/ (as in "moon") and sometimes /ū/ (as in "cute").

A.text: Sam and his mom go to buy a new bike. / "I want the blue one," said Sam. / The shop has a big, blue bike that is true to what Sam likes. / Sam's mom said, "Let's buy it, then get a snack." / They get a bag of fruit and chew on it as they walk home with the new bike.

B.text: Because she had a big meeting, Kate had to buy a new suit. / She went to a shop and got a blue suit that fit true to size. / "This one is right for you," said the person at the shop. / Kate said, "That is true, I will buy this one." / She got a snack of fruit on her way home, glad to have a new suit for the big day.

listen.passage: Choosing an outfit for an important meeting is about more than looking neat — it can genuinely affect how confident a person feels walking into the room, which in turn can affect how well they perform.

tier2.def: sure of yourself, believing you can do something well.
tier2.full: sure of yourself, believing you can do something well.

questions: How might clothing affect how confident someone feels?
What makes you feel confident?

lessons.title: oo (Flex-Decoding Two Sounds)
lessons.goal: Read words spelled with **oo**, which has two common sounds — /o͞o/ (moon) and /o͝o/ (book) — using an explicit flex-decode routine: try one sound, then the other, and check which gives a real word.

A.text: At night, Sam and his dad look up at the moon. / "It is a good, cool night to look at the moon," said Dad. / They sit and look for as long as they can, because the moon is so bright. / Sam has a thing to think of: "What is the moon made of?" / Dad said, "That is a good thing to think of — let's find the answer in a book." / They read a book and find the answer, glad they took the time to look.

B.text: After her shift, Kate likes to sit in her room and read a good book. / When it is cool at night, she gets a hot cup and takes a look at her book. / She took a class once on this same topic, but a book gives her time to think it over. / "I find the answer to a lot of things in a good book," she said. / Soon, she is deep in the pages, glad for a quiet night.

listen.passage: Reading fiction before bed has been shown to help some people unwind, because following a story shifts attention away from the day's worries and toward a different, absorbing world.

tier2.def: so interesting that it holds your full attention.
tier2.full: so interesting that it holds your full attention.

questions: Why might a story help someone unwind before bed?
What do you find absorbing enough to lose track of time?

check.note: dictated sentence 'I took a good look at the book.' -> the app dictates 'look'; flex narration is self-report

rule.title: oo has two sounds
rule.text: Try the long sound first, moon. If it is not a real word, flex to the short sound, book.

lessons.title: -ild, -ind, -old, -ost
lessons.goal: Read words ending in **-ild, -ind, -old, -ost**, a small set of closed-syllable-*looking* words where the vowel is actually long, not short.
lessons.review: all Level 3 vowel teams so far
lessons.heartLine: none new — all 16 Level 3 heart words were completed at L3.08; today is decoding-only.

A.text: It is a wild, cold day, and Sam and his mom go for a walk. / They see a child with a gold kite, and the wind is strong. / "Hold my hand," said Mom, "because the wind is wild today." / Sam is glad she told him to hold on. / They walk the whole way home, and Sam feels most glad once they are back and warm.

B.text: Kate lost her old job when the shop closed, so she must find a new one. / Because she is bold, she does not quit — she sends her whole plan to ten shops. / One shop gets back to her and gives her a spot to start. / "I am so glad I did not lose hope," said Kate, most glad to have a new start. / Kate holds on to the good news the whole day.

listen.passage: When a whole industry changes quickly, many workers must adapt by learning a new skill, which can feel daunting at first but often opens up options a person had not considered before.

tier2.def: something that feels big and a bit scary to start.
tier2.full: something that feels big and a bit scary to start.

questions: Why might learning a new skill feel daunting?
What's something daunting you're proud you tried?

rule.title: Long vowel families
rule.text: In -ild, -ind, -old and -ost the vowel says its name even with no silent e: wild, kind, cold, most.

lessons.title: Level 3 Review
lessons.goal: Consolidate all Level 3 code (VCe for all 5 vowels, drop-e, open syllables, y-as-vowel, soft c/g, ai/ay, ee/ea, oa/ow/oe, igh/ie, ue/ew/ui, oo-flex, -ild/-ind/-old/-ost) and all 16 Level 3 heart words before the mastery check.
lessons.heartLine: all 16 Level 3 words (once, only, very, every, great, eye, busy, people, water, laugh, walk, talk, buy, answer, whole, earth)

A.text: Once, Sam and his family took a whole day just for fun. / At home, Sam ate a bowl of oats and a slice of toast. / Then they went to see a tiger and a robot at a big show. / Sam's eye spotted a huge, gold kite flying high in the sky. / "How very great!" said Sam, and his mom gave him a hug. / Next, they got a snack — a bag of fruit and a sweet, cold treat. / While busy people were there too, Sam felt happy and free. / They went home and read a good book close by the tree. / "This was the best day," said Sam. / His mom said, "I am very glad, too." / They ate a bite of pie, and Sam fell asleep, smiling, once his whole busy, great day was done.

B.text: Once, Kate had a whole day off, and she made the most of it. / She woke up, made a cup of tea, and ate a slice of toast. / At nine, she met her team to help clean up the street — a job she likes since it feels like a great use of a free day. / By noon, the whole team had made the place look neat, and people walking by said, "How nice!" / Kate felt very glad and a bit sleepy, but in a good way. / She got a snack of fruit and a cold drink, then sat and read a good book. / "Today was busy, but it was a great day," said Kate. / Once the sun set, she felt so glad she had spent her whole day well.

listen.passage: People often find that a day spent helping others, even a small task like a neighborhood clean-up, brings a deeper sense of satisfaction than a day spent purely on entertainment. Researchers call this the difference between pleasure and genuine fulfillment.

tier2.def: a deep feeling of satisfaction from doing something meaningful.
tier2.full: a deep feeling of satisfaction from doing something meaningful.

questions: What's the difference between pleasure and fulfillment, based on the passage?
What gives you a sense of fulfillment?

lessons.title: Level 3 Mastery Check
lessons.goal: Administer the graded Level 3 exit assessment and decide: advance to Level 4, or return to a specific lesson for reteaching.
lessons.newToday: none — this is the assessment session
lessons.review: the full instrument is in `../mastery-check.md`; this file is the short tutor script for running it in one sitting.

offline: Connected-text reading (WCPM + phrasing, with the tutor)

ui.teachIntro: Here is a new spelling for a sound. Tap it to hear it.
ui.teachBlend: These letters keep both sounds. Say them quickly together.
ui.teachSuffix: This is an ending. Read the base word, then add the ending.
ui.teachExample: Here it is in a word.
ui.ruleIntro: Here is a rule that helps you read.
ui.attackIntro: A long word. Let's break it apart, step by step.
ui.attackPeel: Tap the parts at the start or end that you know.
ui.attackBlend: Tap each chunk to say it, then put them together.
ui.attackFlex: Is it a real word? If not, try the vowel the other way.
ui.masteryIntro: This is the check for the whole level. Do your best.
ui.masteryPass: You passed! The next level is open.
ui.masteryMiss: Not yet. Let's practise the parts that were hard, then try again.
ui.attackCheckIntro: Show how you read a word you have never seen.
